Fig. 3

The growth state of the cells was observed with an optical microscope. As shown in Fig. 3 (A). The boundary of NC group cells was clear and uniform round or oval in size. In LPS group, the volume of cells increased, many vacuoles and long pseudopods, and their morphology was fusiform or irregular. It has been shown that macrophages are successfully activated when they have more and longer pseudopods, and that their pseudopods increase cell adhesion and phagocytosis. After stimulation of RAW264.7 cells with different concentrations of F2-7 in the experiments, the morphology was changed compared with that of NC normal cells, showing a spindle-shaped and dendritic state, and there was a tendency for the pseudopods of the cells to gradually increase with the increase of concentration. It is shown that F2-7 successfully activates RAW264.7 cells, and pseudopods increase cell adhesion and phagocytosis, and enhance immunoreactivity.
Effects of F2-7 on NO secretion in RAW264.7 cells

NO is an intracellular signalling molecule with oxidative capacity, involved in various pathological and physiological processes, and plays a key role in regulating immune responses. Thus, it can be used as a quantitative marker of macrophage activation. As shown in Fig. 3(B), F2-7 induced a dose-dependent increase in NO secretion (50-200 mug/mL). NO secretion peaked at 7.56 +- 0.33 mumol/mL at 200 mug/mL (P < 0.001), comparable to the levels induced by LPS. These results suggest that F2-7 enhances NO secretion in macrophages.
Effects of F2-7 on phagocytosis of RAW264.7 cells

Phagocytosis is a fundamental function of macrophages, essential for clearing pathogens and tissue remodeling. Fig. 3 (C) demonstrates the effects of different levels of F2-7 on phagocytosis. The LPS group showed a significant increase (P < 0.001) in phagocytic ability of cells by 87.22 % when compared to the NC. Following treatment with distinct F2-7 concentrations, there was a dose-dependent increase in cells' phagocytosis of the neutral red dye. At a concentration of 200 mug/mL, the phagocytic capacity of the cells was 1.87 times greater than that of the NC (P < 0.001), which was like that of the LPS group. The results indicated that F2-7 improved the phagocytosis of RAW264.7 cells.
Effects of F2-7 on cytokine secretion in RAW264.7 cells

The measurement of inflammatory factors such as TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1beta is a crucial indicator of immune response strength and macrophage activation, reflecting the cells' ability to eliminate pathogens and regulate pro-inflammatory responses.The secretion of cellular inflammatory factors in the cell supernatant is shown in Fig. 3 (D, E, F). When LPS stimulated the cells, the secretion of cytokines increased significantly (P < 0.05). In Fig. 3 (D), when the F2-7 concentration was 50 mug/mL, the secretion of TNF-alpha increased by 283.02 % compared with that of the NC (P < 0.001). In Fig. 3 (E), the secretion of IL-1beta was significantly increased (P < 0.05) when the F2-7 concentration was 50 mug/mL compared with the NC, which was 1.5 times higher than that of the NC. As shown in Fig. 3 (F), when the F2-7 concentration was 50 mug/mL, the secretion of IL-6 was elevated by 163.59 % compared with that of the NC (P < 0.001). As the concentration of F2-7 increased, the levels of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta and IL-6 secreted by the cells were almost close to those of the LPS group, and the concentration of 200 mug/mL showed a better effect. The results indicated that F2-7 could enhance the immune activity of the organism by promoting the secretion of cellular IL-6, TNF-alpha and IL-1beta. and found that both oyster peptides and the duck egg white hydrolysate studied by promoted the secretion of NO, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, demonstrating immunomodulatory effects. Therefore, the present study preliminarily investigated the immunological activity of F2-7.

In this study, F2-7 was analyzed by LC-MS/MS, and PEAKS Studio 8.5 software was used for data processing and retrieval analysis. The number of amino acid residues in F2-7 was shown in Fig. 5. The length of F2-7 was mainly heptapeptide, octapeptide, nonapeptide, decapeptide, undecapeptide, dodecapeptide and tridecapeptide, accounting for 86 % of the total sequences. Setting PeptideRanker >0.5 as the threshold, there were 77peptides predicted with bioactivity, which accounting for 47 % of the identified sequences.It was found that most of the peptides in F2-7 contained the characteristic amino acids, up to 80 % or more. The most occurring characteristic amino acids were Pro, Leu, Asp, Ile, Val, Gln and Lys. the most abundant amino acid peptide sequences containing Pro and Leu were 95.12 % and 89.02 %, respectively. In addition, more than 50 % of the peptide sequences had hydrophobic amino acids present at the N and C termini. Therefore, based on the protein plausibility and the presence of more characteristic amino acids we selected six peptides(Table 2) with possible immune activity(LDHVPLP, DHVPLPLP, LDHVPLPLPQ, DHVPLPL, DHVPLPLPQ, HVPLPLP) and then further validated the immune activity by molecular docking and synthetic peptides. The identification information and secondary mass spectra of the six peptides are shown in Table 2 and Fig. S1.

IKK regulates the transcriptional activity of NF-kappaB in response to cellular signals, and thus it has long been assumed that IKK dominates upstream in the NF-kappaB signalling pathway. Therefore, in this study, IKK protein was chosen as receptor protein to study the binding ability of active peptides in F2-7 to determine whether active peptide activate the NF-kappaB signalling pathway. As shown in Table 3, DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP exhibited the favorable interactions with targeted protein IKK (PDB: 2VVY), and the minimum binding energy was -2.75 and - 6.04 kcal/mol, respectively. Moreover, both DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP were buried in the groove of IKK (Fig. 6). The DHVPLPLP formed three conventional hydrogen bonds (Asp-79, Asp-82 and Asn-74) with IKK residues. The HVPLPLP formed eight conventional hydrogen bonds with tree residues (Lys-73, Asn-74 and Asp-78). DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP were stably attached to p65 (PDB:4EYT) by conventional hydrogen bonds with minimum binding energy of -1.64 and - 4.75 kcal/mol, respectively (Table 3). Among them, DHVPLPLP formed two conventional hydrogen bonds with the residue Gln-488 and Asp-497 at distances of 2.2 A and 1.90 A; HVPLPLP formed two conventional hydrogen bonds with Gly-403 and Glu-405 residues of p65 at distances of 3.0 A and 2.2 A (Table 4, Fig. 7). These findings suggested that DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP were the possible cause of the enhanced immune activity of F-7.
The immunoreactivity of DHVPLPLP, HVPLPLP in RAW264.7 cells

(A) Effect of synthetic peptides on RAW264.7 cell viability, (B) NO secretion, (C) neutral red phagocytosis. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)
Fig. 8

DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP were synthesized to verify their proliferative activity in RAW264.7 cells in vitro. The results were shown in Fig. 8(A), DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP could enhance the proliferation of RAW264.7 cells. When the peptide concentration was 200 mug/mL, the most significant effect on cell proliferation was observed(P < 0.001). The proliferation rates of DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP were 222.86 +- 8.76 % and 169.53 +- 7.12 %, respectively. Therefore, the concentration of 200 mug/mL was chosen for the determination of immunoreactivity-related indexes.

The promotion of cellular NO secretion by DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP was extremely significant (P < 0.001) compared with NC as shown in Fig. 8(B). Among them, the effect of DHVPLPLP on cellular NO release was 33.36 +- 0.28 mumol/mL, which was comparable to that of the LPS group. Both DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP significantly increased macrophage phagocytosis by 89.93 % and 42.47 %(P < 0.01), respectively, compared to the NC group as shown in Fig. 8(C). In summary, DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP not only enhanced the proliferation of RAW264.7 cells but also significantly increased NO secretion and phagocytosis. These findings suggest that they have strong immunoreactivity and may play a crucial role in F2-7. This provides a solid foundation for further understanding the immune mechanism of F2-7.
Discussion

Sturgeon cartilage accounts for about 10 % of the body weight and is often discarded or processed into low-value feed. However, sturgeon cartilage is primarily composed of collagen, making it an excellent source for preparing bioactive peptides. Therefore, this study explores the bioactive peptides derived from sturgeon cartilage through enzymatic hydrolysis and investigates their effects on the proliferation of RAW264.7 macrophages, elucidating the potential mechanisms.

Molecular conformation, amino acid composition, peptide chain length, total charge, and other factors affect the biological activity of peptides. Peptides with molecular weights less than 1000 Da exhibit good solubility and can effectively target enzyme cleavage sites. Additionally, they can directly cross the intestinal barrier and produce biological effects on immune cells in vivo. Studies showed that 79.0 % of sturgeon cartilage peptides produced through neutral and alkaline protease treatment have molecular weights below 1000 Da, indicating their biological activity. To enrich the effective components of sturgeon cartilage peptides, these peptides were purified and evaluated using RAW264.7 cells.

When cells are activated, they enhance cell proliferation and phagocytosis, and promote the secretion of NO and cytokines, which constitutes an important non-specific immune response in the body. Macrophages phagocytose pathogens and emit signals that stimulate other immune cell responses. Furthermore, macrophages produce NO, which serves both as an oxidising agent and as an indicator of macrophage activation. The results of the experimental study demonstrate that F2-7 from sturgeon cartilage enzymatic digest significantly enhances the proliferation and phagocytosis of RAW264.7 cells,and promotes NO release. This indicates that the F2-7 fraction activates macrophage proliferation, enhances antigen phagocytosis, and secretes NO to eliminate pathogens. These findings are consistent with previous studies on the immunoreactive peptide SCSP in green clam digestive fluid. Cytokines play a pivotal role in immune responses, with a close association with immunomodulatory functions. Activated macrophages secrete TNF-alpha to recruit natural killer cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils, while IL-6 stimulates antibody production by B cells. The F2-7 fraction has been demonstrated to significantly increase the secretion of cytokines by RAW264.7 cells, including TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6. This suggests that the F2-7 fraction enhances immune responses by directly activating RAW264.7 cells to produce immune factors, thereby achieving immune enhancement.

The NF-kappaB and MAPK signalling pathways are intimately connected with the immune system. The NF-kappaB signalling pathway regulates the expression of various cytokines, and its activity is regulated by kappaB inhibitory factors and kappaB kinase (IKK). Upon stimulation by upstream factors, IKK is activated and phosphorylates IkappaB, ultimately leading to the entry of NF-kappaB into the nucleus The P65 protein activates target genes in the nucleus, where it binds to DNA sequences in the promoters of the target genes and regulates their transcription, ultimately generating effector molecules that are responsible for eliminating pathogens. The present study demonstrated that sturgeon chondropeptide F2-7 significantly enhanced the expression of IKK, P-IKKalpha/beta, p65 and P-p65 proteins. (Please refer to Fig. 5(D-H).) The increase in P-IKKalpha/beta indicates the activation of the IKK complex, which in turn phosphorylates IkappaB, prompting its degradation, release and subsequent activation of NF-kappaB into the nucleus. P-p65 represents a crucial step in the NF-kappaB signalling pathway, enhancing transcriptional activity. Furthermore, sturgeon chondroitin has been demonstrated to activate the NF-kappaB signalling pathway by increasing the level of P-p65, thereby exerting an immune response. Similarly, T1 purified from tuna hydrolysate also activates the NF-kappaB signalling pathway and promotes the immune response, consistent with previous studies. Consequently, it can be postulated that sturgeon chondroitin may play a role in enhancing immunity by activating the proliferation of RAW264.7 cells through the activation of the NF-kappaB pathway and the promotion of the expression of P-IKKalpha/beta and P-p65.

To further elucidate the immune-enhancing mechanism of sturgeon chondropeptide F2-7, we performed molecular docking of peptides identified from F2-7 with NF-kappaB signalling pathway-related proteins (IKK and p65). Based on the minimum binding energy and docking scores, DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP demonstrated high affinity for proteins related to immune response and inflammatory response, suggesting their potential for further analysis. In this study, DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP, which were identified from F2-7, were found to be stably bound to IKK, primarily through conventional hydrogen bonding. This suggests that the stable binding of DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP to IKK may affect the activity of IKK, promote the phosphorylation of IkappaB by IKK, release and activate NF-kappaB, and thus enhance the initiation of the NF-kappaB signalling pathway and enhance inflammatory and immune responses. Furthermore, DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP interact with p65 through conventional hydrogen bonding, which also affects inflammatory and immune responses. This binding directly enhances the DNA-binding capacity and transcriptional activity of p65, which in turn promotes the expression of NF-kappaB-related genes and further enhances the immune response. Furthermore, studies have demonstrated that immunoreactive peptides enriched in hydrophobic amino acids exhibit enhanced immunoreactivity and facilitate intercellular membrane translocation. The proportion of hydrophobic amino acids in DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP is 75 % and 85.71 %, respectively, and has not been previously reported in the database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/, accessed on 25 September 2023). The present study further corroborates the significant immunoreactive potential of DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP. The immunoenhancing effect of F2-7 on RAW267.4 macrophages was achieved primarily through the interaction of these two peptides with IKK and p65 proteins on the NF-kappaB signalling pathway.
Conclusion

This study evaluated the effects of sturgeon cartilage enzymatic hydrolysate on macrophage immune responses using an in vitro cellular model. The sturgeon cartilage hydrolysate was purified through Sephadex G-15, DEAE-52, and preparative liquid chromatography, resulting in the isolation of fraction F2-7, from which two novel peptides were identified: Asp-His-Val-Pro-Leu-Pro-Leu-Pro (DHVPLPLP) and His-Val-Pro-Leu-Pro-Leu-Pro (HVPLPLP). Among them, F2-7, along with peptides DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP, significantly promoted the proliferation and phagocytic activity of RAW264.7 macrophages. Further investigation revealed that F2-7 enhanced the secretion of NO, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6. Additionally, F2-7 activated the NF-kappaB signalling pathway by upregulating the expression and phosphorylation of IKK and p65, thereby significantly enhancing the immune response. These findings provide new insights into the potential applications of sturgeon cartilage. However, the bioavailability of DHVPLPLP and HVPLPLP and their immunomodulatory mechanisms in vivo require further exploration.

passages.text: Evaluating a virtual facilitation workshop with antimicrobial stewardship teams within a cluster randomized stepped-wedge trial
Background

Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASP) often function naturally as facilitators within clinical hospital settings, by working with individuals and teams to reduce unnecessary antibiotics. Within implementation science, facilitation has been studied and evaluated as an implementation strategy that can accelerate and improve fidelity to implementation efforts. This study describes a novel, virtual facilitation strategy developed and served as an intervention within the optimizing perioperative antibiotics for children trial (OPERATIC trial). This paper: (1) describes ASP team's preferences for and use of a facilitation workshop and (2) describes sustained use of facilitation skills throughout the study period.
Methods

Study participants included antimicrobial stewardship team members from the nine children's hospitals that participated in this study and completed facilitation training. All individuals who completed facilitation training were asked to evaluate the training through an online survey. Additionally, site leads were interviewed by the site coordinator every other month and asked about their team's use of facilitation skills throughout the rest of the study period. Survey data were managed and coded in R, and qualitative interview data were analyzed using rapid methodology.
Results

30 individuals, including both physicians and pharmacists, completed the evaluation. Individuals largely rated themselves as novice facilitators (53%). Individuals reported satisfaction with virtual facilitation and identified different components of the workshops as valuable. An additional 108 interviews were performed throughout the study period. These interviews found that facilitators reported using all skills throughout the study period and described varied use of skills over time. All nine sites applied facilitation strategies, team building techniques, and communication/conflict skills at some point during the intervention phase.
Conclusion

We describe the use of virtual facilitation as an acceptable and appropriate strategy to enhance facilitation skills for ASP teams working to reduce unnecessary postoperative antibiotics. Participants reported different useful components of facilitation training and described using differing facilitation skills throughout the trial. Overall, the use of facilitation skills continued throughout the duration of the study period. This paper outlines how facilitation training can be conducted virtually in a way that is feasible and acceptable to clinicians.

Contributions to the literature
This paper demonstrates, for one of the first times, the use of facilitation skills over the course of a project.
This paper specifies the sustainability of facilitation training as an implementation strategy.
This paper outlines the use of virtual facilitation as an acceptable and effective implementation strategy.
Background

Facilitation is described as intentional support provided by an individual to provide necessary resources to enhance care delivery and help overcome barriers to implementation. Although the mechanistic pathways remain undetermined, the strategy has been theorized and studied to enhance the uptake of evidence-based care. Examples where facilitation has improved the uptake of evidence-based care include care coordination, cardiovascular disease treatment, and mental health care integration. Facilitation can be carried out by individuals within the organization where an intervention is being implemented, by individuals external to the organization and/or by those implementing an evidence-based intervention. Conceptual work within the field of implementation science, such as the Integrated Promoting Action on Research in Health Services (i-PARIHS) framework, helps define facilitation, promote skills inherent to a good facilitator, and identify conceptual domains that should be targeted by facilitators to improve the implementation of evidence-based care and overcome implementation barriers. However, little is known about how facilitation can promote de-implementation, or the removal of practices that lack evidence or are known to cause harm within healthcare. Furthermore, facilitation as either an implementation or de-implementation strategy may look different, and by extension providing training on facilitation may require different skills depending on the context and the health issue of focus. As such, it is important to document facilitation strategies to subsequently understand their potential impacts.

A looming public health crisis where successful de-implementation is critical is antimicrobial overuse. To combat this in hospital settings, antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs), often consisting of infectious diseases clinicians, nurses, and pharmacists, intervene and optimize appropriate antibiotic prescribing, to reduce excessive antibiotic use. ASP teams act as natural facilitators, using a variety of implementation strategies to enhance appropriate prescribing across multiple different hospital contexts. These ASPs focus their work at multiple levels, including interventions targeted at clinicians such as audit and feedback, hospital-wide initiatives like treatment protocols requiring antibiotics, and even system-level interventions like prompts and decision support within the electronic health record. Yet, training for ASP teams beyond the biomedical and epidemiological aspects of antibiotic use is virtually non-existent. This remains true despite literature demonstrating the need for social persuasion and navigation of interpersonal dynamics when attempting to change clinical practice within the hospital. Because ASP teams are already positioned to be facilitators for implementing evidence related to antibiotic use, understanding how best to cultivate facilitation skills within ASPs can augment existing efforts by these teams and can enhance their influence within hospital care delivery.

Our primary objective with this evaluation is to enhance our understanding of the ASP team's preferences for and use of a facilitation workshop designed to aid the de-implementation of unnecessary post-operative antibiotics within the pediatric surgical setting. This facilitation workshop was developed and served as an intervention within the optimizing perioperative antibiotics for children trial (OPERATIC trial). For this study, our team developed a virtual facilitation workshop for local hospital antimicrobial stewardship team members to reduce inappropriate post-operative antibiotic prescribing, a known source of excessive antibiotic use in pediatric hospitals. This manuscript reports on the design and content of the facilitation workshops and presents the evaluation of the workshops.
Methods

The OPERATIC trial is a stepped-wedge cluster randomized control trial with nine hospitals, where hospitals were randomized into three clusters (three hospitals per cluster). This trial consisted of six steps lasting six months with all clusters starting in the control arm. The first cluster was switched to the intervention arm of the trial and participated in the facilitation workshop at step 2, the second cluster at step 3, and the third cluster at step 4. Throughout the study, data were collected evaluating post-operative antibiotic use, strategies used to reduce antibiotic use, and clinicians' perceptions of the acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness of the intervention. More details about the overall trial design and data collection approach can be found in our previously published protocol. This analysis used clinicians' facilitation evaluation data to assess knowledge, skills acquired, and satisfaction with the facilitation workshops. We also used data collected every other month focusing on participants use of materials and skills targeted during the facilitation workshop. The Institutional Review Board approved all evaluation protocols.

This study was conducted at nine children's hospitals in the US that are members of the SHaring Antimicrobial Reports for Pediatric Stewardship (SHARPS) Collaborative and the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Project-Pediatrics (NSQIP-P). All hospitals in this study have an active ASP team that includes, at a minimum, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and pharmacist. Hospitals received annual compensation for participating in the study.
Participants

Antimicrobial stewardship team members from the nine hospitals participated in this study. Site leads at each hospital were identified and were responsible for providing a roster of ASP team members at their site. The study team then emailed each of the team members and invited them to participate in the facilitation training. These individuals included physicians, pharmacists, nurses, and other individuals affiliated with the antimicrobial stewardship teams.
Workshop format

These workshops were delivered weekly across one month and consisted of four two-hour virtual sessions, delivered in May 2021, November 2021, and May 2022. The workshop included lectures, discussions, role playing, and networking. Experts in pediatric infectious diseases and implementation science facilitated the sessions. The goal of these sessions was to train ASP teams to act as facilitators in their respective organizations, and each of the sessions was designed to target an aspect of our theoretical model of facilitation. The i-PARIHS framework as well as a review of other facilitation trainings within implementation science informed this training.
Content

The sessions included the following agenda topics: supporting literature for appropriate post-operative antibiotic use, data assessment and interpretation, implementation science principles, communication and conflict, and presenting data/data visualization (Supplementary Material 1). The workshop included discussion among participants about leadership, organizational initiatives, and data reporting. An overview of implementation science principles, specifically focused on facilitation as an implementation strategy, was provided during the first session. Following, in the data assessment and interpretation session, we presented information about NSQIP-P data reports, accessing data, and using data for site specific evaluation. In communication and conflict, we discussed different styles of communication between team members as well as information on conflict styles and approaches to interprofessional conflict. Finally, we discussed site capacity for improvement as well as methods to present data in a persuasive manner. Upon workshop completion, worksheets recapping key educational components were developed and distributed to the sites (Supplementary Material 2).
Data collection

First, immediate evaluation data were collected at the conclusion of the workshop from each participant (post-facilitation workshop evaluation). Second, site leads were interviewed every other month on their use of facilitation and their ongoing impression of the facilitation workshop after completing the intervention (bimonthly process interview).
Measures
Post-facilitation workshop evaluation

To assess the facilitation workshop, participants received a link in their email immediately after the final session to complete an electronic survey on REDCap. The survey was adapted from a prior measure evaluating workshop-based practice facilitation resources. Participants were asked to rate overall satisfaction and perceived individual expertise, with 1 indicating very poor and 5 indicating very good. Questions, on a Likert scale, asked how helpful they believed each component of the facilitation workshop to be with 1 indicating very poor - 5 indicating very good; to rate the overall workshop on the length and utility; and about their anticipated future use of the different components of the workshop, with 1 indicating very unlikely - 5 indicating very likely. Participants were asked to provide any additional commentary or feedback through four open-ended questions: (1) what were the most important things you learned (2) , what else would you add to the workshop (3)? , what would you change about the workshop?, and (4) do you have any other comments/thoughts? The survey took about 10 min to complete.
Bi-monthly process interview

Every other month after facilitation, the research team coordinator conducted an interview with the site lead from each site which was scheduled at the site lead's convenience and conducted via web conference or telephone. During each interview, the site lead was asked about their use of specific facilitation skills and ongoing feedback about the facilitation workshop. A structured interview guide was utilized (Supplementary Material 3). A research team member probed each component delivered during facilitation workshops (data use, data presentation, capacity building, communication/conflict, implementation strategies) during every interview. Interviews lasted approximately 30 min. A research team member took detailed notes in a structured REDCap form during the interview. Due to the nature of these calls, the interviews were not recorded or transcribed. Information about each site's activities was summarized and site leads reviewed the notes and summaries with the study coordinator at the end of the study period.
Data analysis and management

Data were managed in REDCap and analyzed in RStudio. All survey responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Open ended survey questions were analyzed qualitatively. Two members (SM, VM) of the study team independently reviewed the responses and conducted separate content analyses, and one investigator (SM) developed codes for categories generated from the data. The two investigators discussed and resolved the codes.

Finally, the longitudinal interview data were analyzed using rapid qualitative methods. One coder analyzed the questions that individuals answered following the switch into the intervention arm, developed a matrix codebook and then reviewed interview notes to categorize the responses. Individual responses were noted as using each facilitation skill during the interview timeframe or not, and then any extra information was reviewed and categorized. These results were reviewed with the primary facilitation team after completion.
Results
Facilitation workshop evaluation

The facilitation workshop was attended by 36 individuals, with 30 (83%) of them completing the evaluation. There were at least two individuals from each institution that completed the evaluation, such that the responses represented all hospitals participating in the intervention. Individuals who completed the post-facilitation evaluation consisted of 19 physicians (63%), 10 pharmacists (33%), and one person who identified as "other" ASP clinician (3%). Individuals largely rated themselves as novice (53%) or experienced (47%) in facilitation, with none self-identifying as experts.

When individuals were asked about their satisfaction with the workshop, individuals had a median score for the overall workshop of 4 (range 3-5), indicating generally positive satisfaction with the workshop. Participants also agreed that the facilitation workshops could be helpful in planning for the implementation of other programs and practices (median 4, range 3-5). When individuals were asked about their anticipated future use of the workshop components (Table 1), individuals reported a high likelihood that they would use skills from the workshop. High variability from component to component indicated that different individuals found different aspects of the workshop more useful, although each component appeared valuable overall based on aggregated responses.

When asked about the format of the workshop, most individuals indicated that they thought the workshop was the correct length (67%), with 33% stating they would like the workshop to be shorter. When asked about specific teaching elements individuals found useful, individuals reported that both case studies (median 4, range 3-5) and role play (median 4, range 3-5) aided their understanding of the content the most.
Workshop commentary and feedback

Participants described the fundamentals of facilitation and the interpersonal components of the workshop (communication and conflict) as the most useful components of the workshop. We found that the feedback and strategies utilized were similar across hospital settings. Over time, individuals reported using different skills but there was not a pattern to the change over time and instead the use of skills were setting and opportunity dependent. For instance, individuals would use data visualization at times when necessary to present at team meetings, while using communication skills consistently throughout the study period. These were described as foundational concepts to their work, but areas for which they had not received training previously. Teams described this session as useful in how they think about working with other teams, and also in helping consider their own team dynamics and functioning. One participant stated "I enjoyed learning about the various communication styles and conflict styles. Talking through with participants and realizing the types preferred with members of my own ASP team was interesting...". Another session that was described as useful was data visualization, with one participant specifically stating "I learned about different data visualization tips to make my points clearer". Participants reflected that it was especially useful to understand different aspects of data visualization and how to communicate findings to various partners.

Individuals identified more applied content to improve the workshop. Recommendations for future workshops included the addition of more role play, a review of examples and group troubleshooting, and a discussion of each institution's efforts and places for improvement. Additionally, participants requested additional resources in various forms, including handouts, additional follow-up meetings, and copies of information technology resources or presentations.

Participants discussed similar themes when asked about workshop areas they would change, including access to additional resources or more time for application of the concepts through role play and discussion. Participants expressed preferences for logistic changes, such as having the workshop in person or at a different time of the day. Participants described the large time commitment to the workshops and ways to potentially reduce the time burden on ASP teams.

Finally, when asked about additional comments, participants described how the workshops helped facilitate their team functioning and prioritization. Participants reflected on the time spent together as a team and commented that using icebreakers was helpful to build comfort as a group.
Process interview evaluation

The response rate for the process interviews was 100% over the study period. There were 108 overall interviews that were analyzed, representing interviews every other month throughout the intervention period for each site. All nine sites reported using facilitation strategies, team building techniques, and communication/conflict skills at some point during the intervention phase. Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles were asked about as a representation of a specific improvement strategy presented during a workshop throughout the trial (Table 2). Only eight of the sites reported the use of PDSA cycles as a specific tool for reducing post-operative antibiotic use, with an overall frequency of 27 time points out of the 99 possible instances.

When asked to elaborate on the employed facilitation strategies, site leads discussed the use of data in their work and how they were considering analyzing and presenting data to various surgical groups and hospital quality improvement teams. Site leads described the new incorporation of data sources, primarily from the NSQIP-P database that they had been trained on (described above), in their presentations. Additionally, many sites incorporated data visualization and reporting dashboards that were accessible to clinicians. When asked about communication strategies, site leads mentioned their approaches to communication, including their intentionality in meeting planning and preparation of agendas prior to meeting with surgical partners. All the sites also reported planned approaches to getting buy-in and steps they took to build stronger team relationships. Finally, site leads described logistical planning that had changed because of the facilitation workshops, including an ongoing focus on implementation planning.
Discussion

We describe our provision of a virtual facilitation training to ASP teams to enhance their facilitation skills within pediatric hospitals to reduce unnecessary post-operative antibiotic prophylaxis. Our work provides preliminary evidence that facilitation is a strategy that ASP teams find acceptable, and provides skills that teams continue to use over time. Our participants reported finding different aspects of facilitation valuable and employing different facilitation skills at different points in the trial. Team behavior change and use of facilitation continued throughout the duration of the study period. Participants described using facilitation skills at every time point after facilitation training but used different components. This suggests that our virtual facilitation training is a sustainable implementation strategy, even with no additional doses of facilitation training provided to the teams. Furthermore, participants reported that they would be willing to apply these skills to other initiatives in their work. This indicates that facilitation training may have additional benefits beyond our targeted focus of reducing excessive postoperative prophylaxis to improve internal facilitation skills of individuals implementing new evidence-based programs within complex hospital systems.

This study used traditional facilitation workshop components and refined them for delivery to (1) a hospital clinician audience and (2) an exclusively virtual platform. While some of the content in the facilitation training was tailored to our specific context and health concern (i.e., the use of NSQIP-P data to understand excessive postoperative surgical prophylaxis in pediatric hospitals), we feel that the general format (reviewing evidence needs, clinician needs, and contextual influences) is adaptable and valuable for multiple situations.

This study demonstrates how facilitation training conducted virtually is feasible and acceptable to clinicians. While external facilitation, where someone from outside of an organization supports the implementation of evidence-based practice, is routinely done remotely, there are very few examples of conducting training for internal facilitators remotely. This workshop enhances our understanding of the skills and concepts that are acceptable to facilitators within implementation efforts, including communication and conflict training, data presentation, and understanding effective persuasion techniques. Additionally, this provides evidence that supports facilitation as a useful strategy for de-implementation and adds to documented use of facilitation throughout the study period.

Although our original intent was to conduct the workshop in person, the move to a virtual format provided several benefits: (1) enhanced engagement, as participants from all three hospitals in a cluster attended together and discussed problems from their varied experiences; (2) a more cost-effective approach compared to having facilitation trainers travel to each site; and (3) more scalable approach when disseminating this effective workshop to more hospital ASP teams. Respondents reported good overall satisfaction with the workshop. Taken together, this suggests that virtual facilitation is a cost-effective strategy for providing facilitation training.

Feedback on the workshop highlighted ways that this workshop could be improved, including adding practical content and potentially shortening sessions. Based on our experience, we recommend that virtual facilitation sessions should follow a structured agenda, be thematically organized, and be well timed. While participants rated sessions as useful and acknowledged the use of different skills at various points throughout the intervention period of the study, we were only able to address some of the recommendations provided, such as developing fact sheets so that individuals could quickly refer back to materials. Other recommendations could be prospectively integrated in future trainings, including more exercises, opportunities for discussion, and information distribution prior to each session. Maintaining training opportunities in data use/presentation, communication/conflict, team interactions, and tools for rapid improvement would be useful as a supplement and would encourage the use of facilitation skills beyond one-time training.

Virtual facilitation training holds promise for future scale up, but this workshop and evaluation have limitations. First, the evaluation was limited to the nine sites involved in this study, all of which are academic children's hospitals. Virtual facilitation workshops likely have different barriers when conducted in other settings that would need to be analyzed and accounted for. Additionally, this training took place over eight hours, a large time commitment for busy clinicians and practitioners. Identifying time-efficient approaches to conduct these workshops will benefit the broader application of this workshop in future implementation.

While this study addresses the feasibility and self-reported use of facilitation skills following virtual training, future work is needed to link this training to the implementation and clinical outcomes of the evidence-based intervention which we intend to examine in subsequent analyses. If the outcomes of these analyses support the continued use of virtual facilitation training, these programs could be scaled in numerous ways - including to different populations, new evidence-based implementation efforts, other geographical locations, and into non-academic settings.
Conclusion

Facilitation is promising as a de-implementation strategy. Our virtual facilitation workshop provides an adaptable template for others who may be interested in using a similar approach to address either implementation or de-implementation in complex health systems. Additional evaluation linking facilitation to implementation and clinical outcomes is needed to further support the utility of the approach.
